Memory Jogger.new: In \textit{The Chinese Exclusion Case}, a unanimous Court upheld the Scott Act's bar on the return of Chinese laborers holding reentry certificates, holding that a later statute overrides an earlier conflicting treaty and that Congress's power to exclude noncitizens is an inherent incident of sovereignty whose exercise is conclusive on the courts (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/130/581/}{Justia}).

Detailed Case Facts.to: Chae Chan Ping petitioned the U.S. Circuit Court

Procedural History.from: Chae Chan Ping petitioned the U.S. Circuit Court

Judicial Votes.new: The Supreme Court unanimously \textbf{affirmed} the Circuit Court's denial of habeas corpus, \textbf{9--0}. The case was argued on March 28--29, 1889, and decided on May 13, 1889 (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/130/581/}{Justia}; \href{https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/130/581}{Cornell LII}):

Judicial Votes.src: (Four years later, however, Justice Field himself dissented in \textit{Fong Yue Ting v. United States}, 149 U.S.\ 698 (1893), arguing that while Congress enjoyed plenary power to \textit{exclude} noncitizens at the border, resident noncitizens already inside the United States could not be \textit{deported} without Fifth and Sixth Amendment protections (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/149/698/}{Justia}).)

Analysis of Opinions.src: Immediately after 1889, the Court expanded \textit{Chae Chan Ping} into a sweeping edifice of immigration exceptionalism: \textit{Nishimura Ekiu v. United States}, 142 U.S.\ 651 (1892) (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/142/651/}{Justia}) (executive officers' exclusion decisions constitute due process for arriving noncitizens); \textit{Fong Yue Ting v. United States}, 149 U.S.\ 698 (1893) (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/149/698/}{Justia}) (extending plenary power from border exclusion to interior deportation); and \textit{United States ex rel.\ Knauff v. Shaughnessy}, 338 U.S.\ 537 (1950), and \textit{Shaughnessy v. United States ex rel.\ Mezei}, 345 U.S.\ 206 (1953) (upholding indefinite exclusion without a hearing on confidential security grounds).

Even when the Court recognized limited boundaries---such as forbidding criminal hard labor without a jury trial in \textit{Wong Wing v. United States}, 163 U.S.\ 228 (1896) (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/163/228/}{Justia}), or requiring a ``facially legitimate and bona fide reason'' when visa denials implicate U.S.\ citizens' First Amendment rights in \textit{Kleindienst v. Mandel}, 408 U.S.\ 753 (1972)---the core deference survived.

In \textit{Trump v. Hawaii}, 585 U.S.\ 667 (2018), the Court applied deferential \textit{Mandel}-style rational-basis review to uphold Presidential Proclamation 9645 restricting entry from several predominantly Muslim nations.

Examples: Future Applications.src: The United States ratifies a bilateral treaty guaranteeing citizens of Country X visa-free entry for business visits. Two years later, citing economic competition and security fears, Congress enacts a statute barring all Country X nationals from entering the United States and voiding all previously issued visas. A Country X national detained at an airport with a valid visa seeks habeas corpus.

Under \textit{Chae Chan Ping}, the habeas petition fails. Congress's later-in-time statute abrogates the conflicting treaty as domestic law, the visa is a revocable license rather than a vested property right, and Congress's exclusion decision is largely conclusive upon the Judiciary.

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (Later Statute Controls): A Tax Statute Overriding a Treaty.} A self-executing tax treaty between the United States and Country Y exempts Y's residents from U.S. tax on certain interest income. Congress later enacts a statute taxing that income for all foreign recipients, without mentioning the treaty. A Y resident sues for a refund, arguing that the treaty guarantees the exemption. Under the later-in-time rule that \textit{Chae Chan Ping} applied, a treaty and a federal statute stand on equal footing as the supreme law of the land, so ``the last expression of the sovereign will must control.'' The statute governs in U.S. courts; whether the United States has breached its international obligations is a matter for the political branches and diplomacy, not the courts (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/130/581/}{Justia}).
\item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Plenary Power Does Not Shield the Statute): Imprisonment at Hard Labor Without a Jury.} Suppose Congress

Examples: Future Applications.src: enacts a statute authorizing immigration officers, without a jury trial or criminal indictment, to sentence noncitizens found unlawfully present in the interior to two years of imprisonment at hard labor prior to deportation

Under \textit{Wong Wing v. United States}, 163 U.S.\ 228 (1896), while Congress may detain or deport noncitizens administratively, imposing infamous criminal punishment inside the United States triggers full Fifth and Sixth Amendment criminal-procedure protections.

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Opposite-Side (No Deference to the Executive): A Proclamation Contrary to Statute.} Suppose

Examples: Future Applications.src: the President issues an executive proclamation barring all asylum applications at the border in direct contradiction of an existing federal statute (8 U.S.C.\ \S\ 1158(a)(1)) granting a right to apply

\textit{Chae Chan Ping} vested plenary exclusion power in \textit{Congress} (the legislative department); when the President acts contrary to Congress's express statutory scheme, executive power is at its ``lowest ebb'' under \textit{Youngstown Sheet \& Tube Co.\ v. Sawyer}, and courts may enjoin ultra vires executive action without questioning Congress's sovereign authority.

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Fence-Sitter (Uncertain): A Statute Excluding Immigrants of One Religion.} Congress enacts a statute barring the admission of any immigrant who belongs to a named religion. A U.S. citizen whose spouse is denied a visa under the statute sues, invoking the Establishment and Equal Protection principles. \textit{Chae Chan Ping} treated Congress's exclusion judgments, even explicitly racial ones, as ``conclusive upon the judiciary,'' and \textit{Mandel} and \textit{Trump v. Hawaii} apply highly deferential review to entry decisions. But \textit{Trump v. Hawaii} emphasized that the proclamation there was neutral on its face, leaving open whether a facially religious exclusion would receive the same deference. Whether the plenary power tolerates an express religious exclusion has never been decided.
